short.headline: What India's AQI can see, and what it can't
short.dek: India's AQI is useful, but the public history underneath it is thinner than the dashboard feels.
short.body: CPCB exposes more than a live AQI card. A verified raw repository endpoint listed 4,455 daily raw files and thousands more 15-minute, hourly and 8-hour files across 598 station records. But a file path is not pollutant evidence. The downloaded daily audit found 916,083 non-missing PM2.5 station-days, 40 stations with no usable PM2.5, and only 200 stations with usable PM2.5 before 2020. The recent archive is much stronger, but it is still monitored India, not all India.

macha.heading: Okay, so can we trust the AQI?
macha.body: Trust it for what it is: a quick public signal from monitors. Do not treat it as a full history of India's air. Under the AQI, CPCB has raw files, rows and pollutant cells. Those layers do not always line up. Some years have files but no PM2.5. Some current station records show no pollutant value in the latest mirror. The newer public archive is useful, but older PM history and unmonitored places need much more caution.
macha.soWhat: AQI tells you what monitored places can show now; the raw audit tells you where public history is strong enough to inspect.

article.title: What India's AQI Can See, And What It Can't
article.standfirst: AQI is a score from a monitored place, not a map of the air everyone breathes. India's public raw archive is real and deeper than the dashboard suggests, but the inspectable PM2.5 history is late, uneven and city-heavy.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## AQI is a score, not the air

India's AQI is the number most people see first. CPCB's official National AQI material describes it as a score built from pollutant sub-indices. In plain English, each pollutant gets converted into its own index score, then the highest available sub-index becomes the overall AQI. The pollutant behind that highest score is reported as the dominant pollutant. CPCB's public categories run from Good and Satisfactory to Moderate, Poor, Very Poor and Severe.

That is useful design. A single score is easier to read than a table of PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone and other pollutants. But it is also a compression. AQI tells you the public signal from a monitor at a place and time. It does not show every pollutant cell, every missing instrument, every station's history, or whether a public file has enough PM2.5 days for trend work.

This article starts underneath the score. The daily repository audit checked 598 CPCB station records. In 2009, CPCB listed 25 daily station-year files in the audited archive, but only 1 had usable PM2.5. In 2017, there were 504 listed station-year files, but only 80 had usable PM2.5. By 2025, the same audit found 579 listed files and 540 usable PM2.5 station-years. The lesson is simple: files, rows and pollutant cells are different layers of public evidence.

## What raw data can the public download?

CPCB's public raw repository is broader than a daily CSV archive. On 29 June 2026, a direct probe checked 598 station records against the public dataRepository/file-path endpoint for raw data at 15-minute, hourly, 8-hour and daily frequencies. It returned 4,346 listed 15-minute raw files, 4,367 hourly files, 4,396 8-hour files and 4,455 daily files.

That is a real public surface. It matters because the official system is not only an AQI card on a dashboard. It also exposes file paths that can be reproduced by script. But a listed path is still only a listing. It says CPCB has a raw file path for a station, frequency and year. It does not prove that the CSV has rows. It does not prove PM2.5 or PM10 is present. It does not prove the year is complete enough for a trend.

A narrow spot-check confirmed that sub-daily files are not imaginary. For Sanjay Palace, Agra in 2025, the same public download endpoint returned parseable CSVs at all four frequencies: 35,040 rows at 15-minute frequency, 8,760 hourly rows, 1,095 8-hour rows and 365 daily rows. Each file had PM2.5 and PM10 columns with many non-missing values. Treat that as a proof of access, not a completeness audit for every sub-daily file.

The AQI repository is a different case. The CPCB interface has a /repository/aqi route and app-code strings for AQI repository listing and Excel export. In this run, I could not reproduce a stable public AQI audit endpoint comparable to the raw file-path call. Several dashboard routes used an encrypted browser proxy. So the raw repository is treated as scriptably verified here. The AQI repository is treated as visible in the official interface, but not used for locked historical numbers.

## How much PM evidence is actually visible?

The deeper audit downloaded and checked 4,455 daily raw CSVs. Across those files, it found 916,083 non-missing PM2.5 station-days and 872,770 non-missing PM10 station-days. A station-day is one station with one non-missing pollutant value on one date. It is a coverage unit, not a pollution concentration.

The 2017 spike in listed files is the chart's warning label. CPCB lists 504 daily station-year files for 2017, up from 50 in 2016. But only 80 of the 2017 files have any usable PM2.5, and 424 have zero usable PM2.5. Many are CSV shells with daily timestamp rows and blank particulate columns. They are public files, but not public PM2.5 evidence.

The inspectable particle record becomes much stronger after 2020. PM2.5 station-days rise from 15,384 in 2017 to 74,169 in 2020, 153,321 in 2023 and 173,983 in 2025. PM10 follows the same broad pattern in the audited daily files. Do not read that as worsening air. It means more public observations are visible in the repository.

## When is a station-year ready for trend work?

A station-year with one PM2.5 day is visible. It is not a serious yearly record. That is why this audit counts four thresholds: any PM2.5 day, 30 or more days, 180 or more days and 300 or more days.

The distinction is large in the older archive. In 2017, 80 station-years had any PM2.5 day, 76 had at least 30 days, 42 had at least 180 days and only 23 had at least 300 days. By 2025, the four counts were 540, 536, 490 and 444. The gap narrows, but it does not disappear.

The 300-day line is not an official CPCB standard. It is an audit threshold for readers who want a fuller annual history. The point is practical. A dashboard can show a station. A file list can show a year. A trend analyst still has to ask how many actual pollutant days sit inside that station-year.

## Where does the station map go thin?

The station network measures monitored India. It does not measure all of urban India. The CPCB/OAQ station hierarchy used here has 335 distinct city names. Census 2011 counts 4,041 statutory towns. On that denominator, about 91.7 percent, or about 92 percent, of statutory towns are outside this station-list comparison.

This is a place-visibility denominator. It is not a population-exposure estimate. It does not mean 92 percent of Indians lack AQI data. It also does not mean every statutory town needs its own monitor. Some towns are small, some are near larger airsheds, and station-list names do not map perfectly to Census names.

The narrower finding is still important. AQI is a monitor-based public signal. Before we even ask whether a file has PM2.5 cells, many legally urban places are outside the public station-list frame used in this audit.

## Which cities have the deepest PM2.5 archive?

The usable PM2.5 archive is city-heavy. New Delhi has 73,348 PM2.5 station-days in this audit across 25 stations with any usable PM2.5. Mumbai has 41,502 across 28 such stations. Delhi has 39,328, Bengaluru 25,311 and Hyderabad 22,663.

That is not an air-quality ranking. A city can rank high because it has more stations, older stations, fewer missing PM2.5 cells, or all three. A lower-ranked city may be cleaner, dirtier or simply less visible in this public archive.

For national claims, this concentration matters. The public historical archive is strongest where the monitoring network is dense and older. It is weakest where stations arrived late, publish thin histories, or never appear in the public station list used here.

## When did stations first become usable?

First usable PM2.5 year is stricter than first listed file year. It asks when a station first has any non-missing PM2.5 value in the daily repository files.

Only 200 of the 598 station records had usable PM2.5 before 2020. The recent record is much stronger: 508 station-years had usable PM2.5 in 2023, 524 in 2024 and 540 in 2025. Across the full daily audit, 396 stations had at least 1,000 usable PM2.5 days.

That makes the archive good for many current comparisons and weaker for long historical panels. A station appearing in an older repository year does not automatically give you a PM2.5 trend from that year. Sometimes the file exists, but the particle cells do not.

## Where do file years outrun PM2.5 years?

Some station histories look long until you count usable PM2.5 years. Airoli in Navi Mumbai has 17 listed daily years but only 5 usable PM2.5 years, a gap of 12. City Railway Station and Sanegurava Halli in Bengaluru have 11 listed years and zero usable PM2.5 years in the audited daily files.

Across all 598 station records, 40 had no usable PM2.5 in daily files. That splits into 22 records with listed daily files but no usable PM2.5, and 18 records with no listed daily repository file in the audit.

This does not prove a station failed. It says the public daily repository does not support a PM2.5 history for those station-years. For a public audit, that is the difference that matters.

## What does a file with rows but no PM look like?

Some files are not empty. They still do not help with PM2.5 or PM10 history. The examples in this chart have daily rows and zero usable PM2.5 and PM10 days.

Rows are a middle layer of evidence. A file can contain timestamps and gas pollutants such as NO, NO2, SO2, CO or ozone while the PM columns are blank or unusable. For AQI, different pollutants can matter on different days. For a particle-pollution history, PM2.5 and PM10 cells have to be present.

This is why the article keeps file listing, rows and pollutant cells separate. If those are collapsed into one word, the archive looks cleaner than it is.

## What does OAQ add?

OAQ is useful because it mirrors current CPCB data in a cleaner API shape. The inspected CPCB snapshot was generated on 23 June 2026 at 17:40 IST. It had 598 station records. At that moment, 203 records had at least one of the eight main pollutant fields, 139 had all eight, 185 had PM2.5 and 183 had PM10. The other 395 records had no main pollutant value in that snapshot.

That is latest visibility, not deep history. It tells you what the mirror saw at one moment. It does not replace the CPCB repository audit of daily historical files.

The station metadata snapshot also has useful public fields. All 598 records had coordinates, station type, a latest-seen timestamp and an agency or operator suffix in the station name. It did not expose clean commissioning or activation dates. The public can inspect where a station is and who appears to operate it. It cannot cleanly inspect every station's start date from this metadata alone.

## How should you read these numbers?

Read this as a visibility audit, not as a pollution trend. The daily audit used CPCB's public raw repository to list, download and inspect station-year CSVs. The frequency audit counted raw file listings at 15-minute, hourly, 8-hour and daily frequencies. The sub-daily spot-check proved those downloads can work for one station-year. The PM2.5 and PM10 completeness numbers come from downloaded daily files only.

The public surfaces are different. The all-India AQI portal is the current public signal. Advance search is a human-oriented dashboard and export surface. The CPCB raw repository endpoint is reproducible and audited here. OAQ is a clean latest mirror. The AQI repository is visible in the CPCB interface and app bundle, but a stable public AQI audit endpoint was not reproduced for this article.

The caveats are real. This audit does not validate calibration, siting, QA flags, monitor downtime or whether a station represents a whole city. The statutory-town comparison is a place denominator, not a population denominator. The 300-day threshold is an audit choice for trend-readiness, not an official rule.

What India can say with confidence is that public AQI sits on a real monitoring system, and CPCB exposes more raw public data than casual dashboard browsing suggests. What it cannot honestly say from these files alone is that the public can inspect a long, even, all-India PM2.5 record.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: AQI is a public score that converts several pollutant readings into one number and one category, such as Moderate or Poor.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The article asks what that score can show quickly and what it hides about the underlying monitor data.
glossaryBlocks.whyThisKeyTerm: Without this distinction, readers can mistake the AQI card for the full air-quality record.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A pollutant sub-index is the AQI-style score calculated for one pollutant before CPCB reports the overall AQI.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: CPCB's overall AQI is driven by the highest available sub-index, so one pollutant can determine the public score.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The dominant pollutant is the pollutant whose sub-index drives the overall AQI at that place and time.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: It reminds the reader that the same AQI number can be driven by different pollutants in different cities or seasons.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A raw repository file is a downloadable CPCB CSV listed for a station, frequency and year.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The article shows why a listed file is only the first layer of evidence. It may still have empty rows or missing PM cells.
glossaryBlocks.whyThisKeyTerm: Most of the audit turns on the difference between a listed file and usable pollutant data.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A non-missing pollutant cell is an actual value in a pollutant column, not a blank, dash or null entry.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: PM2.5 and PM10 history depends on these cells, not just on whether the CSV exists.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A station-day is one monitoring station with one non-missing pollutant value on one date.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Station-days measure how much public observation exists. They do not measure whether pollution rose or fell.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A station-year is one station in one calendar year.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The article separates a station-year with any PM2.5 from a station-year with enough days to support trend work.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Trend-ready means a station-year has enough non-missing days to be useful for comparing one year with another.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The 300-day threshold in this article is an audit rule of thumb, not an official CPCB quality standard.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A latest mirror is a current copy of what a data source sees at one time, shaped for easier access.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: OAQ helps with current CPCB visibility, but it does not replace CPCB's historical repository.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A statutory town is a legally urban place in the Census frame, such as a municipality or cantonment board.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The town comparison is a place-visibility check. It is not a claim about population exposure or where monitors must be placed.

chartExplainers.visualId: Listed files and usable PM2.5 history diverge
chartExplainers.takeaway: The daily repository grows to 579 listed station-year files by 2025, but the usable PM2.5 history catches up much later.
chartExplainers.detail: This is the article's core chart because it separates three layers: a listed daily file, a station-year with any usable PM2.5, and a listed file with zero PM2.5. The odd 2017 jump is real, but it is a repository-listing finding: CPCB lists 504 daily station-year files, only 80 have any usable PM2.5, and 424 have none. By 2025 the gap is much smaller, with 579 listed files and 540 usable PM2.5 station-years.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It prevents the reader from treating public file availability as public pollutant evidence.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read each year vertically. The red line is listed station-year file paths. The dark line is station-years with at least one non-missing PM2.5 daily value. The green line is listed files where PM2.5 is still zero, so a wide red-dark gap means the repository looks deeper than the PM2.5 evidence inside it.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the red line as operating stations, city coverage or pollution exposure. It is only the count of station-year file paths returned by the repository.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use the legend first. On a small screen, the important move is the red-dark gap in 2017 and the much narrower gap by 2025.

chartExplainers.visualId: CPCB's raw archive extends beyond daily files
chartExplainers.takeaway: CPCB's verified raw endpoint lists thousands of files at 15-minute, hourly, 8-hour and daily frequency.
chartExplainers.detail: The file-list probe returned 4,346 listed 15-minute raw files, 4,367 hourly files, 4,396 8-hour files and 4,455 daily files across 598 station records. A separate spot-check for Sanjay Palace, Agra in 2025 confirmed that sub-daily files can be downloaded and parsed, but this chart itself counts listings only. It does not validate row completeness or pollutant cells inside every sub-daily file.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows that the official public data surface is broader than the dashboard, before the article narrows to the daily PM completeness audit.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar counts file paths returned by CPCB for one raw frequency. The similar bar lengths mean the repository exposes a comparable number of station-year files across frequencies, not that the files are equally complete.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume listed 15-minute, hourly or 8-hour files have the same completeness as the daily files audited in detail.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The bars are close together. The key note is that these are public file listings, not validated pollutant observations.

chartExplainers.visualId: Usable PM observations become broad only after 2020
chartExplainers.takeaway: The audited daily files contain 916,083 non-missing PM2.5 station-days and 872,770 PM10 station-days, with most depth arriving after 2020.
chartExplainers.detail: A station-day is one station with one non-missing pollutant value on one date. PM2.5 station-days rise from 15,384 in 2017 to 74,169 in 2020 and 173,983 in 2025. That is a rise in inspectable observations, not a rise in pollution concentration. The same logic applies to PM10, which is plotted beside PM2.5 as a second particle-coverage check.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shifts the article from file counts to the pollutant cells needed for historical PM analysis.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Follow the lines over time as counts of non-missing daily PM values. PM2.5 and PM10 move together in recent years, which shows that the public particle record becomes much more usable in the 2020s.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not say the line rising means India's air worsened. A coverage line rises when more station-days are visible, even if concentration levels move differently.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The unit is station-days. It is not micrograms per cubic metre and not an AQI score.

chartExplainers.visualId: Trend-ready PM2.5 years lag basic visibility
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2025, 540 PM2.5 station-years had any data, but only 444 had at least 300 non-missing days.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart separates minimal visibility from fuller annual evidence. In 2017, 80 station-years had any PM2.5, but only 23 reached 300 days. By 2025 the gap is smaller, but it still tells analysts not to treat any-data counts as ready-made trend panels.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It answers the question a file audit alone cannot answer: which station-years are substantial enough to compare across time?
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each line raises the minimum bar. The top line counts station-years with any PM2.5 day, while the lower lines require 30, 180 or 300 non-missing days. The spread between lines is the difference between seeing a station-year once and having a fuller annual record.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat 300 days as an official CPCB quality rule. It is an audit threshold chosen to make trend-readiness visible.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare the top and bottom lines first: any PM2.5 day versus 300 or more PM2.5 days.

chartExplainers.visualId: The station list covers only a fraction of urban places
chartExplainers.takeaway: The CPCB/OAQ hierarchy has 335 city names, while Census 2011 counts 4,041 statutory towns.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart is a geography warning, not a monitor-siting prescription. It says about 92 percent of statutory towns are outside this station-list comparison, but it does not say 92 percent of Indians lack AQI data. It also does not say every statutory town needs a monitor, because airsheds and settlement size matter.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It stops the article from quietly equating monitored India with all of urban India.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the smaller station-list city-name bar with the much larger Census statutory-town bar. The gap shows the difference between named places visible in this public station hierarchy and the legal urban frame.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not convert this into a population claim or a one-monitor-per-town rule.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The big bar is the Census denominator. Read the chart as place visibility, not exposure.

chartExplainers.visualId: Deep PM2.5 history is concentrated in a few cities
chartExplainers.takeaway: New Delhi, Mumbai and Delhi dominate the usable PM2.5 station-day archive.
chartExplainers.detail: New Delhi has 73,348 usable PM2.5 station-days, Mumbai has 41,502 and Delhi has 39,328 in the audited daily files. These counts combine station density, station age and missing-cell patterns. They tell us where the public historical archive is deepest, not where air is cleanest or dirtiest.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows that national PM history is city-heavy and strongest where monitoring is dense and older.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars rank cities by total non-missing daily PM2.5 station-days. A city can rank high because it has many stations, long-running stations, better PM2.5 completeness, or some mix of those factors.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not compare these bars as pollution levels. They measure public evidence volume.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Long labels may wrap. Compare bar lengths first, then read city names and counts.

chartExplainers.visualId: Most station PM2.5 histories begin late
chartExplainers.takeaway: Only 200 of 598 station records had usable PM2.5 before 2020.
chartExplainers.detail: First usable year means the first year with any non-missing PM2.5 daily value in the downloaded repository files. It is not the station's commissioning date and not necessarily the first year the station operated. The chart shows why recent PM2.5 comparisons are much easier than long historical panels.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It makes the timing of usable evidence visible, rather than assuming every listed station has a long PM2.5 record.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar counts stations by the first year in which their daily files contain usable PM2.5. A pile-up in recent years means many stations become inspectable for PM2.5 late in the archive.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume a late first usable year always means a new station. Earlier files may exist but have missing PM2.5 cells.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Read this as the start of usable PM2.5 evidence, not the opening date of the monitor.

chartExplainers.visualId: Long file histories can hide short PM2.5 records
chartExplainers.takeaway: Some stations have long listed file histories but little or no usable PM2.5 history.
chartExplainers.detail: Airoli in Navi Mumbai has 17 listed daily years but only 5 usable PM2.5 years. City Railway Station and Sanegurava Halli in Bengaluru have 11 listed years and zero usable PM2.5 years in the audited daily files. These are concrete examples of the file-versus-pollutant gap.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It grounds the article's central distinction at station level, where readers can see named examples rather than only national totals.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is listed daily years minus years with any non-missing PM2.5 for that station. A larger bar means more years where the public repository listed a daily file but did not provide usable PM2.5 history.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not use the gap as proof that a monitor failed. Use it as evidence that the public daily files do not support PM2.5 history for those years.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Station labels are long. The bar value is the number of listed years without usable PM2.5.

chartExplainers.visualId: Daily rows can exist while PM values are blank
chartExplainers.takeaway: Some daily files contain rows but zero usable PM2.5 and PM10 days.
chartExplainers.detail: These representative examples span full-year and partial-year CSVs. A file can contain timestamps and non-PM pollutant columns while both particle columns are blank or unusable. That is why row counts are a middle layer of evidence, not the final answer for PM history.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It makes the missing-cell problem tangible inside actual files, not only in annual summaries.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Bars count daily rows in selected files where both PM2.5 and PM10 usable day counts are zero. The point is not which example is largest, but that non-empty files can still be useless for particle-history work.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not call a file usable for PM history just because it has timestamps or gas-pollutant values.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The chart is about row counts in no-PM examples. Other pollutant columns may still exist.

chartExplainers.visualId: The latest OAQ mirror is a snapshot, not history
chartExplainers.takeaway: In the inspected OAQ snapshot, 598 CPCB station records were present, but 395 had no main pollutant value at that moment.
chartExplainers.detail: OAQ is useful because it mirrors current CPCB data in a cleaner API shape. In the 23 June 2026 snapshot, 203 records had at least one of the eight main pollutant fields and 139 had all eight. That makes OAQ valuable for latest visibility and metadata, but not a replacement for CPCB's historical repository audit.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It separates current mirror access from deep historical evidence.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the bars as one moment in time. The full station-record bar is the denominator; the pollutant bars show how many records had current values in that snapshot; the no-main-pollutant bar shows how sparse a latest mirror can be.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat a latest snapshot as a complete history, or as proof that a station never reports pollutants.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The bars are moment-in-time availability counts, not station histories.

The audit does not validate monitor calibration, siting, QA flags, downtime or whether a station represents a whole city or airshed.
The 300-day threshold is an audit threshold for fuller annual history. It is not an official CPCB completeness standard.
The OAQ snapshot is a latest/current mirror. It should not be read as a deep historical archive or as proof that a station never reports pollutants.
lockedNumbersUsed: CPCB official AQI categories: Good, Satisfactory, Moderate, Poor, Very Poor and Severe; overall AQI is the maximum pollutant sub-index and the corresponding pollutant is the dominant pollutant.

plannedCharts.title: Listed files and usable PM2.5 history diverge
plannedCharts.subtitle: CPCB daily raw repository · listed files, usable PM2.5 years and files with no PM2.5 · 2009-2025
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The core data-poverty point: file availability, row availability and usable pollutant coverage are not the same thing.

plannedCharts.title: CPCB's raw archive extends beyond daily files
plannedCharts.subtitle: Public raw repository probe · file listings at 15-minute, hourly, 8-hour and daily frequency · 598 station records
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: CPCB's public repository exposes raw listings at 15-minute, hourly, 8-hour and daily frequencies, but file listings are not the same as audited pollutant coverage.

plannedCharts.title: Usable PM observations become broad only after 2020
plannedCharts.subtitle: Downloaded CPCB daily files · non-missing PM2.5 and PM10 station-days · 2009-2025
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Counting non-missing pollutant days shows how much usable measurement the repository actually contains.

plannedCharts.title: Trend-ready PM2.5 years lag basic visibility
plannedCharts.subtitle: Downloaded CPCB daily files · station-years by minimum count of non-missing PM2.5 days · 2009-2025
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Trend analysis needs more than one visible PM2.5 day, so this separates minimal visibility from fuller station-years.

plannedCharts.title: The station list covers only a fraction of urban places
plannedCharts.subtitle: CPCB/OAQ city names compared with Census 2011 statutory towns
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The strongest data-poverty statistic is the denominator: most legally urban places do not appear in the station list used for this audit.

plannedCharts.title: Deep PM2.5 history is concentrated in a few cities
plannedCharts.subtitle: Downloaded CPCB daily files · non-missing PM2.5 station-days by city · 2009-2025
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The archive is not evenly distributed. Delhi and New Delhi dominate the long PM2.5 record.

plannedCharts.title: Most station PM2.5 histories begin late
plannedCharts.subtitle: Downloaded CPCB daily files · first year with any non-missing PM2.5 value, by station
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This shows the start date for usable station histories, rather than the first year a station appears in the repository.

plannedCharts.title: Long file histories can hide short PM2.5 records
plannedCharts.subtitle: Downloaded CPCB daily files · listed file years minus years with any usable PM2.5, by station
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This is the audit check behind the article: some stations have long file histories but much shorter usable PM2.5 histories.

plannedCharts.title: Daily rows can exist while PM values are blank
plannedCharts.subtitle: Selected CPCB daily files with rows and zero usable PM2.5 or PM10 values
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Concrete examples keep the caveat honest: some files are not empty, yet still have no PM2.5 or PM10.

plannedCharts.title: The latest OAQ mirror is a snapshot, not history
plannedCharts.subtitle: OAQ CPCB latest snapshot · generated 23 Jun 2026 at 17:40 IST

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
